official_title: Shall the Constitution of Georgia, for the purpose of protecting family farmland, be amended so as to increase the maximum acreage to qualify for assessment and taxation as a bona fide conservation use property from 2,000 acres to 4,000 acres?
plain_summary: Georgia taxes enrolled farm and timber land at its value as farmland, not what a developer would pay. Owners sign a 10-year promise to keep it that way. This doubles how much land one owner can enroll, from 2,000 to 4,000 acres.
yes_means: One owner could enroll up to 4,000 acres of farm or timber land in the conservation-use tax program instead of 2,000.
no_means: The cap stays at 2,000 acres per owner.
current_law: Article VII, Section I, Paragraph III(e)(1) of the Georgia Constitution lets the legislature set a lower, current-use tax value for 'bona fide conservation use property' (agricultural and timber land) up to 2,000 acres of a single owner. Enrolled land is assessed at 40 percent of its current-use value under a 10-year covenant. The 'bona fide residential transitional property' limit of five acres is unchanged by this amendment.
fiscal_impact: No official state fiscal note is published for Georgia constitutional amendments. The AJC reports opponents' concern that it 'could reduce local government and school property tax revenue' because more land would be taxed at the lower farm value; no dollar estimate has been published. The state's General Fund is not directly affected because property tax is local.
pass_threshold: simple majority of votes cast on the measure
confusing_wording_note: The question starts with 'for the purpose of protecting family farmland.' That phrase is a stated purpose, not a rule. The amendment doesn't define 'family farm,' and the higher cap applies to any owner who qualifies for the program, not only family farms.

supporters_case.text: Sponsor Sen. Sam Watson (R-Moultrie) says the conservation-use rules date from the 1980s when farms were smaller, and that raising the cap helps keep family farms in business.

opponents_case.text: Critics quoted by the AJC say it could reduce local government and school property tax revenue and give large or corporate farm operations a tax break they don't need.

official_title: Shall the Constitution of Georgia be amended so as to require that all probate court judges be elected in nonpartisan elections?
plain_summary: Probate judges handle wills, estates, guardianships and marriage licenses, and today they can run with a party label. This would make all probate judge elections nonpartisan, like elections for Georgia's superior court, state court, Court of Appeals and Supreme Court judges.
yes_means: Probate judges would run in nonpartisan elections with no party label, like Georgia's other judges.
no_means: Probate judges would keep running in partisan elections with a party label.
current_law: Article VI, Section VII, Paragraph I(a) of the Georgia Constitution requires nonpartisan elections for superior court and state court judges (4-year terms) and Supreme Court justices and Court of Appeals judges (6-year terms). Probate judges fall under 'all other judges,' who are chosen the way they were on June 30, 1983, which in practice means partisan county elections unless a local law says otherwise.
fiscal_impact: No official fiscal note. The change affects how candidates appear on the ballot, not the court's budget. Under current Georgia law, nonpartisan judicial races are held in May with the primary, not in November.
pass_threshold: simple majority of votes cast on the measure
confusing_wording_note: If you see the 9-1-1 fund called Amendment 2 somewhere, go by the official ballot: probate judges is Amendment 2 and the 9-1-1 fund is Amendment 3. A yes vote doesn't remove any sitting judge; it changes how future probate judge elections work.

supporters_case.text: Sponsor Rep. Kimberly New (R-Villa Rica) says party labels conflict with the judicial code of conduct and that judges 'should serve the law, not a political party.' The measure passed with 94 percent of Republicans and 85 percent of Democrats voting yes, per Ballotpedia.

opponents_case.text: No organized opposition was found. The AJC and Augusta Press explainers list no arguments against. Some legislators voted no.

official_title: Shall the Constitution of Georgia be amended so as to authorize the General Assembly to dedicate certain existing revenues, including revenues reallocated by law, to a nonlapsing fund to be used exclusively for the expansion, maintenance, and operation of emergency 9-1-1 systems in this state?
plain_summary: This lets lawmakers create a protected fund that can only be spent on 911 systems, including upgrades so 911 can take texts, photos and video. Money left over at year end stays in the fund. It doesn't raise any fee or tax by itself.
yes_means: The legislature may create a permanent, protected fund for 911 systems and steer existing 911 fee revenue into it.
no_means: No dedicated 911 fund; 911 money keeps flowing through the regular budget and local distribution as it does now.
current_law: Article III, Section IX, Paragraph VI of the Georgia Constitution limits dedicated funds and lets unspent money lapse. Georgians pay a $1.50 monthly 911 charge on phone lines, which is currently distributed to local 911 centers. The amended FY2025 budget put $5.7 million of seed money toward Next Generation 9-1-1.
fiscal_impact: No official fiscal note. The AJC reports approval 'would not immediately change the current $1.50 cellphone 911 fee'; a later law would decide what revenue goes in. A House study committee recommended shifting the existing local 911 charge into the statewide fund. Athens Politics Nerd notes this could move money from local distribution to a state fund, though spending would likely stay about the same.
pass_threshold: simple majority of votes cast on the measure
confusing_wording_note: A yes vote doesn't create the fund. It lets lawmakers create one later by passing a law. 'Certain existing revenues, including revenues reallocated by law' means the money would come from the 911 fee you already pay, possibly moved from your county to the state.

supporters_case.text: Supporters, including the Georgia Emergency Communications Authority and the Georgia Municipal Association, say Georgia's 911 setup has changed little since 1968 while most calls now come from cell phones, and a protected fund is needed to finish the statewide upgrade. The resolution passed both chambers unanimously on final passage.

opponents_case.text: No organized opposition was found. Senate Democrats briefly blocked it in March 2026 over process, not substance (Sen. Derek Mallow: 'until we can find a way to work together in this chamber, I'm going to vote no'), then voted for it. Athens Politics Nerd flags a possible loss of local control over 911 fee revenue.
